pedagogy.summary: Orbital mechanics for ages 12-13 should be taught conceptually, not algebraically. The central, counter-intuitive idea is that an orbit is CONTINUOUS FREEFALL: a satellite is always falling toward the planet, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it just as quickly, so it keeps missing. Newton's cannonball thought experiment is the canonical bridge — fire a cannonball faster and faster from a mountaintop until it falls all the way around. From there, build two more ideas: a GRAVITY ASSIST (a spacecraft steals a tiny bit of a planet's orbital motion in a close flyby to gain speed for free), and the conceptual heart of the ROCKET EQUATION — because a rocket must carry the fuel it hasn't burned yet, the fuel needed grows explosively (exponentially) as you demand more speed change, which is why getting to space is so hard. Keep it about momentum-versus-gravity balance and 'falling sideways', reserving the maths for later.
bestPractices: Lead with the paradox 'astronauts are not weightless because there's no gravity — they are in constant freefall', to confront the dominant misconception head-on
Use Newton's cannonball as the spine: increase launch speed step by step so the child sees crash → suborbital arc → circular orbit → ellipse → escape emerge from one variable
Frame orbit as a tug-of-war between sideways momentum and gravity's inward pull: too slow and you spiral in, too fast and you fly away, just right and you circle
Teach gravity assist as borrowing motion from a moving planet — a slingshot that costs the planet an imperceptible amount and gives the craft a lot
Convey the rocket equation qualitatively with a 'fuel to carry fuel' spiral: each extra bit of speed needs disproportionately more propellant because you must lift the unburned fuel too
Separate the two forces cleanly — thrust changes the orbit, gravity shapes it — so children don't think engines must fire continuously to stay up
keyRepresentations: Newton's cannonball diagram: a mountaintop cannon with a family of paths from crash to full orbit to escape
'Falling but missing' picture: the straight-line path the object would take without gravity vs the curved orbit, with the ground curving away
Momentum-vs-gravity vector picture: forward velocity arrow plus inward gravity arrow producing a curved path
Gravity-assist trajectory: a spacecraft's bent path speeding up as it swings past a moving planet
Rocket 'fuel-carrying-fuel' staging bar showing propellant mass ballooning as target speed rises
commonMisconceptions: 'There's no gravity in space, that's why astronauts float' — gravity in low orbit is nearly as strong as on the ground; they float because they and their ship are falling together
'Rockets need to keep their engines on to stay in orbit' — once at orbital speed, no thrust is needed; the craft coasts in freefall indefinitely
'Orbits are perfect circles' — most are ellipses; a circle is just the special case of exactly the right speed
'Going up is the hard part of reaching orbit' — the real challenge is going sideways fast enough; altitude alone gives you a suborbital hop that falls back down
'A gravity assist gets energy from nothing' — the craft borrows orbital momentum from the planet, which loses an unmeasurably tiny amount in exchange
'More speed just needs proportionally more fuel' — because you must carry the fuel you haven't burned, required fuel rises exponentially with desired speed change

learn.summary: Conceptual (non-algebraic) orbital mechanics for ages 12-13. The core, counter-intuitive idea: an orbit is CONTINUOUS FREEFALL — a satellite is always falling toward the planet, but it moves sideways so fast that the curved ground falls away beneath it just as fast, so it keeps missing. Newton's cannonball thought experiment is the canonical bridge (fire faster from a mountaintop: crash → suborbital arc → circular orbit → ellipse → escape, all from one speed variable). Build two further ideas: a gravity assist (a spacecraft borrows a tiny amount of a planet's orbital momentum in a close flyby to gain speed), and the qualitative heart of the rocket equation (because a rocket must carry fuel it hasn't burned yet, propellant needed rises steeply/exponentially as demanded speed change increases). Frame throughout as momentum-versus-gravity and 'falling sideways', reserving maths for later.

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: one speed dial from crash to escape
feedback: If the ball crashes, you are going too slow — its path curves down into the ground faster than the ground curves away; increase the speed.

At the circular-orbit setting, point out that the straight-line overlay shows the ball steadily dropping below where it 'should' be — that drop IS the falling, and the sideways motion is why it never arrives.

If the ball escapes, it had too much sideways speed (at or above escape speed) for gravity to bend its path into a closed loop — gravity still acts and keeps slowing it, but can't curve the path back around.
Connect back to astronauts: a person inside this orbiting ball would float, not because gravity is gone, but because they are falling together with it.
activities.rationale: The relationship is dynamic and single-variable; letting a learner vary one speed and watch the trajectory morph makes 'falling sideways' something observed rather than asserted. The straight-line overlay makes Newton's first law and the continuous bending by gravity concrete.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
Without gravity an orbiting object would fly off in a straight line (Newton's first law); gravity continuously bends that straight-line path into the orbit
Newton's cannonball thought experiment (fire faster and faster from a mountaintop until the projectile orbits) is the canonical conceptual bridge for orbit-as-freefall
learnerActions: Stand a cannon on a mountaintop above a round planet and set a single SPEED value, then fire and watch where the projectile goes.
At low speed, observe the cannonball arc down and crash into the ground; raise the speed and watch the arc get longer but still fall back.

Keep raising the speed until you find the setting where the ball curves downward exactly as fast as the planet's surface curves away, so it sweeps all the way around into a circular orbit (and would come back and hit the cannon from behind).
Push past that setting to see the circle stretch into an ellipse, then push higher still to watch the ball escape and not return.

Compare the orbit against a faint 'no-gravity straight line' overlay showing the path the ball would take with gravity switched off, and note how far it 'falls away' from that straight line each second.
State in your own words why the orbiting ball is still falling even though it never hits the ground.
activities.intendedInsight: Orbiting is just falling and continuously missing the ground: one launch speed, varied smoothly, produces crash, circular orbit, ellipse and escape; gravity bends the would-be straight-line path into the orbit.

activities.title: The momentum-vs-gravity tug-of-war
feedback: If a learner invokes an outward (centrifugal) force balancing gravity, redirect: gravity is the only force here; it bends the straight-line sideways motion into a curve, and that curve is the orbit.

Too slow: gravity curves the path down into the ground, so it falls back and crashes. Faster than circular speed but below escape speed: the path still closes, but stretches into an ellipse. At or above escape speed: gravity can't curve it enough to close the loop. Just right for a circle: the curve exactly follows the planet's surface shape.
Note that gravity sets how the path accelerates (curves), not the direction the ball is currently travelling — the ball keeps moving sideways while gravity pulls it inward.
activities.rationale: Naming and drawing the two influences confronts the common 'balanced outward force' misconception directly and reinforces that only gravity acts on the ball in flight in this idealised model.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
Without gravity an orbiting object would fly off in a straight line (Newton's first law); gravity continuously bends that straight-line path into the orbit
learnerActions: For a chosen launch, sketch or identify two arrows at the projectile: a forward (sideways) velocity arrow and an inward arrow pointing at the planet's centre for gravity.
Predict, before firing, whether a given speed will crash, circle, stretch into an ellipse or escape, and justify using the two arrows.

Explain why 'too slow' falls back and crashes, why a bit faster than circular speed stretches the orbit into an ellipse, why 'much too fast' (at or above escape speed) flies away, and what 'just right' for a circle means.
State explicitly that gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (in this idealised model) — there is no outward force holding it out.
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit results from sideways momentum plus a single inward gravitational pull that continually curves the path; there is no real outward force balancing gravity.

activities.title: Gravity assist: borrowing a planet's motion
feedback: If a learner says the assist 'creates' energy, clarify: it is a transfer — the planet's orbital motion is the source, and its loss is unmeasurably small because it is enormously more massive.
Note that the net speed gain depends on the planet moving; a flyby of a stationary body returns the craft at the same speed it arrived (in that body's frame) and gives no net boost.
activities.rationale: Seeing the speed readout change during a timed flyby makes the momentum transfer tangible; the navigator dialogue adds mission-level reasoning about why routes are chosen.
learnerActions: Time a close flyby of a spacecraft past a MOVING planet and watch a speed readout before and after the encounter.
Experiment with the timing/geometry of the flyby to make the craft gain speed, and describe what happened to its path.
Explain where the extra speed comes from — the craft borrows a tiny share of the planet's orbital momentum, while the planet loses an unmeasurably tiny amount.
Optionally, discuss with a mission navigator planning a probe to Jupiter why it might slingshot past Venus and Earth first instead of flying straight there.
activities.intendedInsight: A gravity assist is not free energy from nothing: a spacecraft exchanges momentum with a moving planet during a close flyby, gaining useful speed while the planet's change is imperceptible.

activities.title: Fuel to carry fuel: why rockets are mostly propellant
feedback: If a learner expects 'more speed just needs proportionally more fuel', have them compare two Δv settings and read off how disproportionately the fuel grows.
Reinforce the loop: more fuel adds more mass, which needs yet more fuel to move — this compounding is why the growth is so steep.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner drive the Δv and watch propellant balloon conveys the exponential intuition without algebra, directly targeting the proportional-fuel misconception.
sourceClaims: The rocket equation implies propellant needed rises exponentially with desired velocity change because a rocket must carry unburned fuel — taught here qualitatively
learnerActions: Set a target speed change (Δv) and watch the required propellant amount build up.

Increase the target Δv in steps and observe that the propellant needed grows faster than in proportion — doubling the demand always takes more than double the fuel, and far more than double once the Δv is large.
Explain in your own words why this happens: the rocket must lift and accelerate the fuel it hasn't burned yet, so extra fuel also needs its own fuel to be carried.
Describe why this means getting to orbit is hard and why large rockets are mostly fuel by mass.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a rocket carries its unburned fuel, the propellant needed rises steeply (exponentially) with the demanded speed change — the qualitative heart of the rocket equation.

activities.title: Consolidate and predict
feedback: For 'astronauts float': the correct reason is that they and the ship are falling together in continuous freefall, not that gravity is gone (gravity in low orbit is still about 90% of surface strength).

For engines: once at orbital speed in the idealised vacuum model nothing slows the sideways motion, so no thrust is needed to stay in orbit — thrust changes an orbit, it does not hold the craft up. (Real very low orbits have slight atmospheric drag, so craft such as the ISS need occasional reboosts.)
activities.rationale: Prediction and explanation tasks check the ideas after the interactive exploration; this is consolidation, not first exposure, since it tests rather than generates the insight.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
learnerActions: Order a set of launch outcomes (crash, suborbital arc, circular orbit, ellipse, escape) from slowest to fastest launch speed.
Set the speed that produces a circular orbit and justify the choice.
Answer 'why do astronauts float?' and explain why it is freefall, not absent gravity.
Explain why a spacecraft already at orbital speed does not need its engines running to stay up.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the falling-sideways model to new cases: predicting outcomes by speed, and explaining floating and engine-off coasting.

constraints: Keep the treatment conceptual, not algebraic: momentum-versus-gravity and 'falling sideways', reserving the Tsiolkovsky maths for later.
Lead with the paradox that astronauts float because they are in constant freefall, not because gravity is absent; low-orbit gravity is still strong (around 90% of surface value).
Separate the two forces cleanly: thrust changes an orbit; gravity shapes it. Avoid implying engines must fire continuously to stay in orbit.
Avoid introducing a real outward (centrifugal) force: gravity is the only force bending the straight-line sideways motion into the orbit in this model.
An ordering/prediction task checks understanding but does not generate the 'aha' of seeing an orbit emerge; use it to consolidate after exploration, not as first exposure.

A static annotated cannonball diagram can name the paths and label the freefall idea, but a fixed picture cannot show speed continuously morphing the trajectory; treat it as a reference scaffold, not a substitute for the dynamic exploration.

A 3D view better conveys inclination and the out-of-plane geometry of transfers and slingshots; the clean 2D plane is clearer for the straight-line-versus-curve comparison, so 3D is proposed as an extension after the 2D intuition is built. Neither is universally required.

A navigator/engineer dialogue can motivate route choices and mission reasoning; seeing the counter-intuitive geometry in motion may help learners grasp it, so dialogue is proposed alongside the moving model rather than as a replacement for it.
Where a slingshot or orbit model uses an idealised, frictionless vacuum, state that it is a model; real missions involve additional factors such as atmospheric drag during launch.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two source claims are marked unverified in the original row: the Newton's-cannonball framing (classic Newtonian mechanics, not confirmed against a fetched page) and the exponential rocket-equation claim (Tsiolkovsky, not confirmed against a fetched page). They are standard physics-education content but were not independently verified here.

The '90% of surface gravity' figure and '~8 km/s' orbital speed come from the row's assessment fields and are consistent with standard low-Earth-orbit values; they were not re-verified against a source this session.

The original phrased orbit as a 'balance'/'tug-of-war' between momentum and gravity; this is a useful intuition but can be misread as implying a real outward force. Activities explicitly correct this by stating gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (idealised model), consistent with the row's own centrifugal-force error pattern. Source claim[0] is retained as an exact copy and keeps the looser 'balance' wording.

The original's 'too slow and you spiral in' phrasing is imprecise for a frictionless two-body model: an under-speed launch follows an ellipse that crosses the surface and crashes rather than spiralling inward (which would require drag/orbital decay). Corrected to 'falls back and crashes' in the activity and feedback.

Self-audit of logic: a resultant (gravity) force sets acceleration/curvature, not the current direction of travel — the cannonball keeps moving sideways while gravity pulls it inward; the straight-line overlay and an explicit feedback note make this clear rather than implying gravity 'drags' the ball straight down. No arithmetic claims were asserted in learner-facing tasks.
One medium-efficacy constraint was softened from an unqualified necessity claim to proposed/may wording, since relative medium effectiveness is untested here.

probeDeeper: Roughly how strong is gravity at the Space Station's height compared with the ground — near zero, or almost as strong?
If gravity is still pulling the Station down, why doesn't it hit the Earth?
What would happen to the Station if you could magically switch gravity off?
Why doesn't a spacecraft in orbit need to keep burning fuel to stay up?
assess.correctAnswer: There is still strong gravity at the Station's height — about 90% as strong as at Earth's surface — so it hasn't escaped gravity at all. The Station IS falling toward Earth constantly; it just moves sideways so fast (about 8 km per second) that as it falls, the curved Earth keeps curving away beneath it and it keeps 'missing' the ground. That continuous falling-while-missing IS an orbit (Newton's cannonball). The astronauts float because they are in the same continuous freefall as the Station, falling together — not because gravity is gone. No engine thrust is needed to stay in orbit, because nothing slows the sideways motion in the vacuum.

errorPatterns.pattern: the Station floats because there's no gravity that high up, or it has escaped Earth's gravity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity is about 90% as strong at that height; the Station is falling, not gravity-free — reconnect to gravity acting across space to hold the Moon and planets.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Station stays up and astronauts float because there is no gravity at that height.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attributes orbit and floating to absent or escaped gravity

errorPatterns.pattern: you have to keep the engines firing constantly to stay in orbit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Once at orbital speed the Station coasts in freefall — no thrust needed, since nothing in the vacuum slows its sideways motion.
errorPatterns.distractor: A spacecraft has to keep its engines running the whole time to stay in orbit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child thinks continuous thrust holds the spacecraft up

errorPatterns.pattern: orbit is where Earth's gravity and some outward force exactly balance
errorPatterns.nextMove: There is no outward force — gravity is the ONLY force, continually bending the straight-line sideways motion into a curve; that curve IS the orbit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child invokes a real outward (centrifugal) force balancing gravity

responseLevels.gap: Says there's no gravity in orbit, that it's escaped or balanced, or that engines hold it up.
responseLevels.full: Explains orbit as continuous freefall — strong gravity plus fast sideways motion so it keeps missing Earth — that astronauts float because they fall with the Station, and that no thrust is needed once at orbital speed.
responseLevels.partial: Knows gravity is still present and the Station is 'falling', but can't articulate the sideways-motion 'keeps missing Earth' mechanism, or still invokes a balancing force.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Astronauts on the Space Station float around, and the Station keeps circling Earth without its engines running. Is that because there's no gravity that high up, or because the Station has escaped Earth's gravity? If neither, what is actually keeping it up — and why doesn't it just fall down? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'no gravity in space' idea persists even among older students. A child who holds it says the Station floats because gravity is gone or has been escaped or balanced. A child who understands orbital motion says gravity is still strong and the Station is in continuous freefall, moving sideways fast enough to keep missing Earth. The 'why' tier forces the falling-sideways model.
